headline: Israel buries flagship climate risk portal, sparking fear of policy reversal on resilience
deck: The country’s most advanced tool for mapping climate threats now sits idle under the Environment Ministry, raising alarms over future disaster preparedness.
body: Israel’s Environment Minister has quietly sidelined the nation’s flagship climate risk portal, a decision that strips policymakers of their primary instrument for mapping heatwaves, droughts, and infrastructure vulnerabilities. The move effectively halts a years-long effort to quantify Israel’s exposure to climate disasters, leaving government agencies without a coordinated source of truth. Critics warn the decision erodes the country’s ability to plan for extreme weather events already intensifying across the Mediterranean. The portal, developed under previous administrations, was designed to aggregate real-time data on water shortages, wildfire spread, and urban heat islands.

The decision was confirmed by Haaretz, which reported that the ministry has not assigned staff to maintain or update the platform since the current minister took office. Internal emails cited by the outlet show requests for access to the portal were redirected to outdated spreadsheets and fragmented agency reports. The minister’s office has not publicly explained the rationale, though allies in the ruling coalition have dismissed the portal as “bureaucratic overreach.” Climate advocates argue the sidelining reflects a broader retreat from evidence-based environmental policy.

Israel has invested heavily in climate resilience over the past decade, positioning itself as a regional leader in water conservation and renewable energy. The portal, launched in 2021, integrated satellite feeds, soil moisture sensors, and flood models to produce localized risk scores for every district in the country. Municipalities used its projections to reroute power lines away from wildfire-prone ridges and to prioritize school renovations in flood zones. Without it, local officials say they are flying blind as temperatures rise and rainfall patterns shift.

A former senior official in the Environment Ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, called the move “a step backward for national security.” The official noted that Israel’s coastal cities, power plants, and desalination facilities are particularly exposed to sea-level rise and storm surges, risks the portal quantified with increasing precision. “You can’t manage what you can’t measure,” the official said. “Now we’re back to guessing.”

The sidelining comes as Israel faces mounting climate pressures. The country recorded its hottest July on record in 2023, while the Dead Sea region saw flash floods that collapsed roads and trapped travelers. Scientists at the Israel Meteorological Service have warned that compound events—heatwaves coinciding with droughts—could overwhelm emergency services within years. Yet without a centralized risk tool, agencies are forced to rely on ad-hoc warnings and international alerts.

Environmental NGOs have condemned the decision as a political signal rather than a policy choice. “This isn’t about efficiency,” said a spokeswoman for the Israel Union for Environmental Defense. “It’s about deprioritizing climate action to make room for other agendas.” She pointed to recent legislative moves that weakened oversight of industrial pollutants and delayed renewable energy targets. The ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

The decision also complicates Israel’s international commitments. The country pledged under the Paris Agreement to slash greenhouse gas emissions 27 percent by 2030 and to mainstream climate risk into national planning. Experts say the portal’s abandonment undermines both goals by removing a key tool for tracking progress and allocating resources. Analysts at the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change have emphasized that risk portals are not optional infrastructure—they are prerequisites for resilience.

For now, the portal’s data remains accessible to researchers and journalists, but without updates it risks becoming obsolete within months. A climate scientist at Tel Aviv University who used the tool to model heat-related mortality called its sidelining “a failure of governance.” “We know the risks,” the scientist said. “What we don’t know is whether anyone in power still cares enough to prepare.”
